report:
Mostly **no** for prevention. The best evidence is the Cochrane review of placebo-controlled trials using ≥0.2 g/day: in ordinary-population trials, regular vitamin C did **not** reduce cold incidence (29 comparisons, 11,306 participants; general-community pooled RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.94–1.00), and the authors concluded routine supplementation is not justified. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23440782/ https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD000980_vitamin-c-preventing-and-treating-common-cold

The key exception is people under brief extreme physical/cold stress—marathon runners, skiers, soldiers on subarctic exercises—where five trials (598 participants) found risk roughly halved (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.35–0.64). For everyone else, regular vitamin C may modestly shorten colds/reduce severity, but that is not prevention. NIH’s fact sheet similarly does not support routine use to prevent colds. https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/VitaminC-HealthProfessional/

Bottom line: don’t take vitamin C expecting fewer colds unless you fit the extreme-exertion subgroup; adequate intake is reasonable, but prophylactic megadoses lack support.
